why: It gives us the institution we need for a town map - that a theater is a licensed establishment, that the magistracy decided how many there were, and that the number ended up very small, capped because a big timber hall in a townhouse block was a fire the city could not fight - which is why a settlement gets one licensed playhouse or none rather than a row of them. That is our inference, not the article's: it describes the capital only and says nothing of how many houses a provincial town had; and the cap was on licensed houses flying the yagura tower - it records that unlicensed shrine-ground theaters (miyaji shibai) played alongside them in simple huts, roofed only over the stage and barred from the draw curtain, revolving stage and hanamichi, and that the provinces had their own local theater (jishibai). Its limits are that this article carries the encyclopedia's own warning that its sources are unclear; that the licensing was an Edo city policy under one government, so we take the arrangement rather than the number itself; and that the count is dated - four houses by the 1670s, three only from 1714 - so "three" is not true of the whole period. It also shows the licensed houses standing together - two on one street, and all three sent in 1842-43 to one site of some ten thousand tsubo far outside the outer moat, a move the Tenpō Reforms ordered to purge the pleasure trades from the castle town rather than a fire rule - which is the capital's theater street. Of a house's own measures it gives only a footnote's stage opening of 6 ken (about 11 m) for the late-Edo Nakamura-za, and the teahouses each house kept in the 1760s (Nakamura-za 16 large and 15 small, Ichimura-za 10 and 15, Morita-za 7 large); those footnotes are unsourced like the rest of the article.

It gives what our maps take about cremation grounds: that Edo's temples burned the dead in their own precincts, and that the shogunate moved those precinct crematoria together to a designated site near the Kozukappara execution ground, at the city's edge, in 1667 after the smoke reached a shogunal grave visit (for this the article cites the 1735 Zoku Edo sunago and Asaka and Yagisawa's 1983 monograph Kasoba); and the forms of the fire bed - most grounds open-air to the end of Edo, with a roofed bed and a walled snow-country hut appearing around mid-Edo. Its limits are that its passages on the fire-bed forms and their mid-Edo dating carry no footnote of their own, so they are the article's word, likely drawn from Asaka and Yagisawa's Kasoba (1983), which it lists but which we have not read; that it describes Japan only, and says cremation before Meiji was not the national norm - common where Jodo Shinshu followers were many and in crowded cities, while elsewhere, and among the ruling class after about 1800, the dead were buried - so a place on our maps need not have a cremation ground at all; and that the episode is the shogunal capital's - twenty-odd temple crematoria in two wards, moved as a group by government order, in a city of a million - so a provincial town's one or two burning grounds is an inference from it rather than a reading of it.

It gives the dimensions of a domain school's ground - about 120 by 60 ken for the original Aizu school - which sets the size band a school occupies on our capital maps, and it shows archery and martial halls standing on such a ground. Its limits are that the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources, which matters because we take a dimension from it; that Aizu's was one of the foremost domain schools in the country, so it bounds the top of the range; that the halls it names belong to the 1987 reconstruction rather than the original; and that it states no rule pairing a lecture hall with a drill hall.

Our small urban temples are drawn as places with named patron households rather than as public monuments, and this is the article that defines that relationship. Its named examples are at the very top of society - the Tokugawa house's temples at Kan'eiji and Zojoji, the Date house's Zuihoji - so applying the pattern to the modest households of a town carries it down several tiers, and the registration system it describes is an Edo administrative institution, where an earlier setting inherits only the patronage. It is definitional rather than quantitative: it fixes what a small temple is for and who pays for it, and carries nothing about how large such a temple is, where it sits on a street, or how many a town holds.

It gives the relation between a shrine's approach road and the highway - the road running from the busy highway to the hall, the gate-front town along it, and highways bent to bring them nearer a shrine - which is what places a shrine and its approach on our town maps. Its limits are that none of its three references is attached to the sentences we quote, so it is an unsourced definition rather than a referenced finding; that it is a general Japanese case with no date; and that it supports the relation between road and hall and no distance or width.

We use it to explain why a flooded paddy might be drawn carrying a green film rather than clear water, which is a visible surface feature with a reason behind it. The productivity numbers it quotes come from modern agronomy, so we cite the practice and the mechanism rather than any yield.

We use it as an upper anchor for how large a capital monastery could get, which is what keeps our own biggest temple from being drawn too small. Its limits are that the sentence we quote is cited to the temple's own website, an institution's description of itself rather than a count or a study; and that this was one exceptional court-supported monastery, so it bounds the top of the range and says nothing about an ordinary temple.

We use it for one thing only: where a city put its dead, which turns out to be at the edge, in named districts on the outward side of the settlement, and that is a placement rule a map can follow. It is one city's arrangement, so it tells us the shape of the custom rather than any measured distance, and Kyoto is a capital, so the pattern is applied to smaller places by analogy rather than by evidence.

Japanese dictionaries are good evidence that the deep-mud wet paddy we draw was a distinct and familiar kind of field, common enough to have its own everyday word. The limits are that a dictionary defines a word rather than measures a field, so there is no depth, no extent and no date here; anything more than the term and its sense comes from other entries in the record.

It gives the L-shaped farmhouse with the stable under the same roof, projecting from the dwelling and warmed by the kitchen hearth, which is what our cold-country farmhouse variant is drawn from. Its limits are that it is a regional house type of Iwate, not the ordinary farmhouse of the country; that the stable's projection from the SOUTH face is the article's description of the Tono basin in particular, where the article also records both right- and left-handed forms, so the compass side is a local observation and not a property of the type; and that the article associates the form with the upper stratum of the village - headmen and prosperous farmers - so drawing it as the ordinary farmhouse would misstate its standing.

Our farmhouses are thatched, and this article gives the physical reason their roofs are drawn steep: thatch is pitched steeply to shed rain, and the coarser and thicker the stems the wider the gaps and so the steeper the pitch required. The limit is that it gives no number - no angle, no degrees - so the specific pitch on our roofs is our own choice within a requirement the article states only in words.

We use it for that plain definition of a polder and for the chessboard look of one from above, which is exactly what a general-audience geography magazine reports well. The more particular claim that a polder's internal channels take crescent and bow shapes and are gated at their ends is not on the page that can be read, so nothing on our maps rests on it.

This settles a question a map has to answer before anything else: whether a domain's government sits inside a fortress or in a walled mansion in a town, and the answer turns out to follow from the lord's rank rather than from the size of the domain. It tells us which building held the government and nothing about what that building looked like - no plan, no size, no arrangement of offices, all of which we take from elsewhere.

It gives one small-to-middling domain's castle where the everyday business of government was transacted in the second-bailey palace rather than the keep, which is what puts the working offices of our capitals in the bailey. Its limits are that the building named is the rebuild of 1861, a very late Edo datum standing for the whole period; and that two castles are a thin base for a rule - the other, Kawagoe, is a different article this key does not link.

Our castle towns have to place the great retainer mansions and to decide where government was actually done, and this article supplies both in general terms: the karo decided matters in joint council at a hall such as the hyojosho, and their mansions stood near the castle. Its limits are precision - "near the castle" is not a distance, and it names no ring or block of the town, so the concentric arrangement our maps draw is our reading of a general statement rather than something this article says.

It is the one source with numbers behind our rule that a farm pond's shallow shore is reeded, giving the zoning of reed and cattail by water depth and bank slope, and it is what shows that a working reservoir does not have a bare margin: a Kagawa study it reports found more emergent and floating-leaved species where ponds are dredged and their algae cut, and it is the ponds that have fallen out of use that lose their variety, so a working reservoir does not have a bare margin. It is a professional-society review reporting recent surveys of ponds still in use rather than primary evidence of its own, and the correlation it reports comes from a single prefecture, so we take a pattern of where plants stand from it and not a figure about how a premodern pond looked.

It describes how a reservoir's embankment is kept - cultivation forbidden, the bank mown and burned, and the sun-loving grassland herbs that result - which the record offers as a confirmation of the rule that reeds keep off a raised, tended bank. Its limits are that the passage we use carries no citation on the page, so its weight comes from the prefectural and ministry sources cited beside it; that the practice is a maintenance regime with no date attached; and that the page never mentions reeds - it contrasts the tended bank's herbs with the tall grasses and kudzu of a neglected one - so "herbs, not reeds" is our inference from the regime and not the page's statement.
unsettled: The maintenance regime is undated, so whether it is premodern or present-day evidence is a judgment.

why: That banding is what we use to draw the edge of a village pond, and it is ecology rather than history, so it changes little between a modern pond and a premodern one of the same shape. The zonation figure is credited to a book we were not able to read, so we cite the banding from this document at one step from its original.

It is the check on an easy mistake, that a pond a village works must be the barren one: the impoverished pond in this comparison is the urban concrete one, while the farmed pond in its living landscape is the rich one. So we take the direction of the contrast - managed is not the same as bare - and none of its counts appear on any map.

It is our evidence that a reed bed is a harvested resource rather than scenery - cut in winter for yoshizu blinds, thatch, summer shoji and standing screens, and left to deteriorate when nobody cuts it - which is what a reader is told when they click the reeds on a map. Honest limits: everything it describes is a lake or river reed bed on Lake Biwa, so we cite it for lake and river reeds only; nothing we could read puts that harvest economy on the margins of a farm pond, and our record says so rather than stretching this page to cover it.

This one is cited for a caution rather than a fact: the article's own account of the assessment converting other crops and produce into their rice equivalent is what stops us from reading a domain's rice rating as evidence that its land was mostly wet paddy, which would put paddy on maps that should carry dry field. It is used here only for the definition of a fiscal convention, and for no measurement at all.

We use it for that ratio, one headman to one village, which is the general rule our settlements follow. It has a specific gap that matters here: it never says whether its "village" is the natural cluster of houses or the larger administrative unit that could contain several, which is the very question at issue, so it fixes the ratio and leaves the unit open.

Household size is the number that turns a population into a count of houses on a map, and this entry vouches for the source those numbers come from and for the direction of travel - households in the regions studied got smaller over the period. It gives no absolute household figure at all, so we use it only to confirm the method and the trend and take actual numbers from elsewhere.

unsettled: The page is unreadable, so its period is a guess from a modern forestry bureau's description.

why: It gives the two facts a bean plot on a map turns on - that the plant is an annual, replanted every year, and how tall it stands - and the first is a constant of the species. Its limits are that the height it gives, 50 to 125 cm, describes the crop as bred and grown now - the article gives a separate modern-cultivar figure and says nothing about landraces - so the drawn height is a modern-crop range used because no premodern measurement of the plant could be read.

We use it only for the shape and the color of the plant, so that a bean plot on a map is drawn as something a reader could tell from rice, and a plant's habit and leaf color are not much changed by the century. Its limits are that it describes modern varieties in the American Great Plains and Corn Belt, bred shorter and more even than the landraces an East Asian farmer would have sown, so we treat the height band as an approximation rather than a measurement of our setting's crop.

It gives the true diameter of the thing our oversized wellhead glyph stands for, from a municipal museum describing the well-digging of its own famously watery district, and the figure is not really local - a shaft has to be about that wide for a digger to work at the bottom of it. The limits are that it is the dimensions of hand-digging we take from it and not a dated historical measurement; the English here is this project's translation of the Japanese.

The record cites it for one sentence, its definition of the word - trees planted so as to encircle the perimeter of the homestead - which is the picture a reader is likeliest to meet and the one the surveyed form does not bear out, since the grove stands on one or two windward sides. Quoting it is how the record shows that the encircling reading is a gloss on the TERM rather than a description of what was built, and the same page's dating of the name to the middle of the Edo period is what makes the word old enough to matter for a setting pitched before Meiji - though the page hedges that itself, saying the name SEEMS to have become established by then, and gives no source for it. Its limits are that its definition is a working one written for owners rather than a finding, and that it speaks of Miyagi alone.

We use it for the construction of the shaft that the well glyph in a yard stands for - firm ground will hold a bare dug shaft, while ground liable to collapse needs a lining (idogawa) - and for the related point that wells were often held jointly rather than by one household, because digging one was expensive. Its limits: it describes Japanese wells in general, modern ones included, and dates nothing it says, so it does not establish that the lined shaft or the shared well is the Edo-period form rather than a general Japanese one; it says nothing about where in a yard a well is placed, so that decision on our maps rests on other sources; and it is in Japanese, quoted here in our own translation.
unsettled: The page is undated, so premodern evidence is the best fit rather than a settled one.

why: Drying racks are one of the few farm fixtures that change the look of a settlement's fields for a few weeks a year, and this is a plain description of where they usually stand - mainly in the paddies and dry fields after the harvest - which is what we needed in order to place them. The article says "mainly", not "only": it supports the field as the usual place and is silent about the farmyard, so keeping racks out of our yards is our reading, not its rule. It describes Japanese practice as recorded in the modern era; hand-harvested rice was dried this way for centuries, but the article does not date any of its statements, so we take from it only the general placement and not any figure.

It settles the one thing we need, which is where such a stone stands: on the road and at a boundary rather than inside a farmyard. It describes one highway in particular, so we use it for placement and for what the stones are, never for a count or a measurement.

We use it for vocabulary - what the formal front gate of a walled residence is called and what one looks like - when naming and drawing the gates on our compound plans. Its limits: its illustrated example is a single eighteenth-century gate; and the term as JAANUS defines it belongs to a warrior's residence, so nothing about a farmstead's gate or about what such a gate meant for a farming household's standing can be sourced to it.

It shows that Japanese topographic maps give bamboo its own symbol beside broad-leaved forest, conifers and bamboo grass, which is the convention our maps borrow when they draw a grove differently from a wood. Its limits are that it is a hiker's blog explaining the legend rather than the agency's own legend document, though that document is public and linked from the page and is the closer source; and that it is a map drawing convention, not a physical claim.

unsettled: A landform-and-water pattern older than the era, but the deck states it as a modern general pattern.

why: We use it for two plain facts of a custom that is still visible on farms today and that we draw on every homestead: the shrine is tiny, and it sits at a corner of the grounds rather than at the center. Because the page names no compass direction, which corner we put it in is our own choice.

It answers why a farmstead has a manure pit at all and why the stuff sits there instead of going straight onto the fields, which is what justifies drawing a separate pit on the plot rather than treating it as part of the privy. It gives no storage times or pit dimensions, so the size we draw the pit at is our own decision.

This is the single most useful fact for laying out a lowland village: houses and dry fields go up on the levee, which is the only naturally drained ground for miles, and the paddy goes into the backswamp behind - a rule the article states directly for long-established Japanese settlements. So we take the siting principle from it and not any measurement; and it describes Japanese alluvial lowland, so it applies to our river-plain settlements and says nothing about hill or fan country.

It gives the plan and the height of the largest shrine sanctuary in Japan, the upper bound for a shrine hall's size. Its limits are that its one height is for the Izumo sanctuary of 1744, the national outlier rather than a provincial shrine, and that it gives no dimension of the plan - only that the 1744 hall's floor is laid with 60 tatami mats, an area and not a plan, and since when it does not know - so the plan's size in ken is this project's reading.

It supplies one number, the working clearance a modern regulator requires around a large open fire, from which the cleared ground around a capital's pyre is derived. Its limits: it governs a recreational bonfire rather than a funeral pyre; the fifty feet is a regulator's safety margin keyed to a code-defined fire, not a measurement of anything; and the record's own finding is that Edo's crematoria were moved for their smell rather than their sparks and that the real premodern practice was containment - a stone hearth inside a walled ground - so this distance stands in for a containment practice the record documents, as a reasoned choice on our part and not as evidence about any real settlement.

It is honest evidence that a nucleated farm village in East Asia lays deep walled lots in rows along an east-west street with subordinate lanes crossing it, and honest evidence of what such lots measure - about one to two, mostly 30 m or less wide by 50 m or less deep, commonly 300 to 500 square metres, with the working yard in front of the house rarely deeper than 20 m. What it cannot be used for is anything that depends on the village not having been rebuilt: its own central finding is that the plan was remade by a Chinese state resettlement in about 1968, which is when the ground behind the lots was opened and given streets. Everything it reports about the older form comes at second hand from two mid-twentieth-century works. The building culture is Manchu and Han northeastern, shaped by the kang and by a cold-climate demand for south-facing rooms, and the authors note the Manchu form had become hard to tell from the Han by 1933.

One sentence says where a courtyard household kept its animals and why: in north China the east wing takes the western sun in summer and the cold northwesterly in winter, so it is unfit to live in, and in Shaanxi courtyard houses wealthy households mostly used it to store grain or as a kitchen or a horse stable. The article gives that use for Shaanxi alone: its own section on the side wings says that in a Beijing courtyard house the east wing is the higher-ranked one, lodging the eldest son and his wife, so the stable in the east wing stands for the northwestern house and not for every northern one. That is the branch of this project’s byre knob where a household owning its team stables it inside its own yard, and it gives the map a NAMED side instead of "one wing". Its limits are provenance: this article’s own reference for the sentence is a folklore dictionary page surviving only as a 2007 capture, so no scholarly survey stands behind it. A Shaanxi or Hebei vernacular-architecture survey would be the better footing. The article's gate at the southeast and its courts by household and ground describe the Beijing courtyard house as the Yuan, Ming and Qing developed it. Its references there are mostly 2000s newspaper and web pages; one architectural historian's handbook (Zhang Yuhuan, 2000) backs the room counts. Its deepest court, about 77 m, is the spacing of Beijing's lanes: a figure from a capital's street grid, not from a town's or a village's plot.

We use it for a single figure that tells us how recent a dense temple landscape actually is - six thousand Jodo-sect temples in existence in 1696, nine tenths of them founded from the sixteenth century onward - which is the check on how many precincts a settlement of a given age should carry. The count covers one sect rather than all of them, and the page carries no all-sect total, so we do not put one on a map.

We use it for two things - that small shrines traditionally had no dedicated priest and were kept by the parishioners in rotation, and the parts of a shrine precinct (the torii marking the sacred ground, the temizuya beside the approach, the shamusho). "traditionally" is its own word and carries no date.

We use it for the tōya system - no full-time priest, the members serving as priest by yearly turn - which is the pure-Shinto village arrangement the setting does not draw. Regional in its examples (the Kinki), undated in this sentence.

We use it for the sentence that the jingūji where the bettō resided was itself called a bettō-ji - the monk lived at the shrine's temple. An office with many senses; only its shrine-temple sense is used.

We use it for the arrangement itself - the shrine's rites performed in Buddhist form by the bettō, the head of the shrine monks, from the temple where he lived - and for its end at the Meiji separation. No count of how many village shrines had one.

We use it for the shasō - the "shrine Buddhist monk" who was at once shrine priest and Buddhist monk - and for the scale of the 1868-1874 demolitions, which is what makes the pre-1868 fused form invisible today. Its figure of 30,000 is its own estimate; it treats the great shrine-temple complexes and says nothing of how common a jingūji or a resident shasō was at an ordinary village shrine - the step this record marks as uncounted.

We use it for the order that defrocked the shasō and bettō and sent them back to their shrines as kannushi - the clearest statement that a monk had been serving the shrine. The policy, not the village.
We use it for the sizes a honden of this style takes - one to eleven bays, one and three the commonest - which grounds the one-bay sanctuary. It says nothing about which villages had which.

We use it for two statements: that it is the most common honden form in the country, and that a one-bay front makes it an ikkensha. Undated, and "most common" is a statement about the surviving national stock rather than a premodern census.

We use it for the statement that the full seven halls belonged only to large temples with many monks and that most small temples had only a main hall and a bell tower - the floor of the program and the reason the bell is a knob. Its limits: a statement about the small temples that stand today, read back onto a premodern program; the bell knob's presence rule is labeled a guess for that reason.
We use it for the absence of an office at small shrines, whose business was done at the administrator's private house - which is why the program has no office building.
